l: mourning, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: is_expressed_by Chorus of Captive Women [through lamentation and bodily self-wounding] The Chorus mourns Agamemnon with torn clothing, cries, tears, and blows upon the breast. Electra brings offerings, lays her grief before the tomb, and recognizes the signs of mourning in the lock of hair.

l: Electra’s prayer, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Electra asks Hermes, the gods below, and Earth to convey her appeal to Agamemnon. She prays for Orestes’ return, restoration of the household, punishment of the slayers, and a purer soul and hand for herself.

l: Clytemnestra’s dream, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra’s dream depicts her birthing and nursing a full-fanged serpent that wounds her breast; it foretells the serpent’s revenge and the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus.

l: the serpent, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: The serpent, Clytemnestra’s dream child, is born, swaddled, and nursed by her, draws blood, represents Orestes, and signifies her death.

l: the offerings, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra sends offerings to Agamemnon’s tomb after a terrifying dream to appease the dead, but Orestes judges them unable to atone for murder.

l: the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: The entity is Orestes’ planned and carried-out vengeance killing of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, ordered by Apollo and justified as retaliation for Agamemnon’s death. Orestes and Pylades first plan to enter the palace disguised as Phocian travelers. Orestes resolves to kill Aegisthus, if he rules in Agamemnon’s place, and Clytemnestra. After gaining entry, Orestes kills Aegisthus for adultery and then kills Clytemnestra, cutting her neck with a sword, for plotting Agamemnon’s murder. The killing of Clytemnestra becomes the central charge of matricide: the Furies demand punishment, while Orestes and Apollo defend it as commanded vengeance. It is judged in the trial of Orestes as blood guilt.

l: Kilissa, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Kilissa, Orestes’ nurse who cherishes him from infancy, mourns his reported death, then, persuaded by the Chorus, summons Aegisthus unguarded.

l: Delphi, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: is_a land [containing the shrine] Delphi is associated with the Pythian cave and Apollo’s oracle. Orestes leaves as a banished wanderer to seek purification and refuge at Apollo’s shrine there.

l: the sword, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes appears with his sword dropping blood after killing Aegisthus. He uses it to kill Clytemnestra as well.

l: Orestes’ madness and vision of the Furies, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: After the killings, Orestes says that his spirit is breaking free of its restraint and that madness is driving him. He sees Gorgon-like, snake-haired Furies that the Chorus cannot see and flees toward Apollo’s shrine.

l: freedom restored to Argos, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: is_a political restoration [following the deaths of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus] The Chorus declares that Orestes has restored freedom to Argos by removing its two usurpers. It celebrates the hoped-for return of rightful rule and the lifting of the palace’s oppression.

l: The Pythian Priestess, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: A seeress of the Delphic oracle, she uses the sacred chair and recounts the shrine’s prophetic succession before fleeing in terror from Orestes and the sleeping Furies.

l: Athena, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena, also called Pallas, is a goddess, daughter and child of Zeus, associated with his thunderbolts and bearing Athena’s aegis. She is Athens’s patron, guardian, ruler, and protecting goddess, and guards the Pythian Temple at Delphi. Her central action concerns Orestes: summoned to Athens, she protects him while recognizing the Furies’ claim and judges blood-guilt too grave to decide alone. She creates a permanent sworn council-court on Ares’ Hill, summons twelve citizens, and directs them toward law, reverence, and fear. When their votes are equal, she casts the deciding vote, declares Orestes free from blood-guilt, and establishes the trial as a lasting institution. She then persuades the Furies not to harm Athens, founding a covenant that grants them sanctuary, worship, honor, and influence over the city’s fertility and prosperity.

l: the Pythian Temple at Delphi, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo’s prophetic shrine with central altar and priestess’s sacred chair, where she receives oracles, Orestes seeks refuge, and Apollo orders the Furies away.

l: Athens, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athens is Pallas’ city and a sanctuary of the Greek gods, containing the Acropolis and the Temple of Athena. Orestes must flee there as an uncondemned suppliant, where Athena establishes a permanent court with Athenian judges to decide blood guilt. Apollo’s favor supports the court, and Orestes’ alliance binds Argos against attacking Athens. Athens then receives the Furies as honored powers, gaining their dwelling, worship, protection, and blessings. Through justice, divine favor, and the new settlement, it receives Victory, prosperity, and freedom from civic strife.

l: the central altar, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: The central altar is where the Priestess sees Orestes crouching for refuge with a bloodied sword and an olive branch. Orestes clings to it while the Furies sleep nearby.

l: the blood of Clytemnestra, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: is_sought_by the Furies [as the basis of vengeance] The blood of Clytemnestra is the basis of the Furies’ pursuit of Orestes. They say that they follow the scent of a mother’s blood and seek vengeance for the matricidal killing.

l: vengeance, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Vengeance is embodied by the Furies as an ancient duty of blood repaid with blood. After Clytemnestra’s death, it drives them to pursue Orestes from place to place, renewed by her Ghost and disputed by Apollo in Athens.

l: the trial of Orestes, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: The trial of Orestes is an Athens judgment over whether Orestes must be punished for killing Clytemnestra. Apollo sends him to Athena’s city to seek release from suffering. Athena appoints twelve Athenian judges and requires sworn witnesses and evidence. Orestes admits the killing, while Apollo argues that Zeus commanded it. The judges divide equally, and Athena’s deciding vote acquits Orestes, establishing his atonement. The balanced result preserves the Furies’ honor and supports their reconciliation with the younger gods.

l: Temple of Athena, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Temple of Athena is a shrine on the Acropolis in Athens, containing Athena’s statue; Orestes seeks sanctuary there, and Athena’s arrival frames his dispute with the Furies.

l: the statue of Athena, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: is_a_refuge_for Orestes [as a sacred suppliant place] Orestes clings to the statue of Athena as a sacred suppliant seeking protection and judgment. The Furies find him there and claim that his refuge cannot free him from the consequences of matricide.

l: the twelve Athenian citizens, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: are_judges_in the trial of Orestes [appointed to decide the cause] Athena calls the twelve Athenian citizens to attend and learn the ordinance governing the judgment. They are identified as the Athenian body for whom the new tribunal and its laws are established.

l: the twelve judges, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: The twelve judges, sworn members of the council-court, cast equally divided votes in Orestes’ trial until Athena’s additional vote acquits him.

l: the council-court of judges, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: A sacred, sworn tribunal established by Athena on Ares’ Hill, the council-court permanently judges bloodshed, guards Athens, rejects gain, punishes swiftly, and remains watchful.

l: Ares’ Hill, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Ares’ Hill is named as the site of the new council-court. Athena connects its name with the place where the Amazons camped and sacrificed to Ares during their attack on Athens.

l: the vote of the judges, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: is_equal half condemning and half freeing Orestes [with Athena’s deciding vote] The judges’ votes are divided equally between condemning and freeing Orestes. Athena’s vote is added to the votes for acquittal, and Orestes is declared free from blood-guilt.

l: fear and reverence, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: protect Athens [by restraining injustice] Athena commands that Reverence and Fear enter the hearts of free citizens and restrain them from injustice. She says that divine fear and holy dread help preserve justice and the state.

l: lawful government, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: requires fear and reverence [to prevent both lawlessness and tyranny] Athena calls for government in which no person lives without restraint by law and no person is subjected to tyranny. She also insists that the monarchy of Awe remain within the walls, so that respect for law and divine fear protect the state.

l: the younger gods, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: overrides the ancient gods [in the judgment concerning Orestes] The younger gods are accused by the Furies of overruling and tearing away ancient right. Athena answers that the outcome of the trial was fair and that the Furies have not been dishonored.

l: Athena's citizens, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena’s citizens worship the Furies, receive Justice, and are promised protection and prosperity if they honor and loyally escort them to a new shrine.

l: Athena's covenant with the Furies, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena’s covenant grants the Furies eternal sanctuary, honor, worship, and influence; in return, they accept Athens, bless fertility and prosperity, and renounce blight and civic vengeance.

l: the Furies' sanctuary, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: The Furies’ sanctuary is promised within the heart of Athens, near sacred shrines, and is later identified as a shrine beneath the Areopagus. Athena leads them there in a torchlit procession so that they may protect the land from fate and harm.

l: civic strife, The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: is_forbidden_in Athens [by the civic settlement] The settlement promises that Athens will no longer hear the sound of civic sedition, bloodshed, and vengeance. The Chorus instead pledges common friendship between people and states, turning hostility into blessing.

l: Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: This unit surveys Aeschylus and seven surviving dramas, stressing dates, lost trilogies, recurring mythic and theological narratives, and the limits imposed by missing sequels and fragments. It follows four plays in particular. The Suppliant Maidens begins with Io’s persecution by Hera, her restoration by Zeus in Egypt, and the descent of Danaus and Aegyptus from her line. Danaus’s daughters flee Egypt rather than marry Aegyptus’s sons and claim Argos as their ancestral home. King Pelasgus hesitates because protection may mean war, but the Argive people unanimously grant sanctuary; when the Egyptian herald attempts to seize the women, Pelasgus enforces the decree. The Danaids thank Argos while fearing the conflict to come. The Persians turns to Xerxes’s invasion of Hellas. Atossa’s dreams and omens precede a messenger’s report that the Persian fleet has been defeated at Salamis and the retreating army devastated. Darius’s ghost condemns Xerxes’s bridge across the Hellespont and his disregard for the gods, warning Persia not to attack Hellas again. Xerxes returns in torn clothes, and he and the elders lament the dead and the collapse of Persian power. The Seven against Thebes depicts Eteocles organizing defenses against seven Argive attackers. As a spy reports each champion and gate, Eteocles assigns six defenders; at the seventh he chooses to confront his brother Polynices himself. Despite the Chorus’s warnings and its account of the inherited curse on Laius’s and Oedipus’s house, the brothers kill one another. After Thebes survives, Eteocles is honored in burial but Polynices is forbidden burial; Antigone vows to bury Polynices, dividing the Chorus. Prometheus Bound presents Zeus’s newly established rule as ruthless. Bound by Hephaestus for giving fire and arts to mortals, Prometheus lists the knowledge he gave humanity and insists that fate will ultimately limit Zeus. Oceanus offers cautious help, while the Oceanides pity Prometheus. Io arrives in her suffering, and Prometheus predicts both her restoration and that her distant descendant will free him. Refusing Hermes’s demand for the secret marriage that will cause Zeus’s fall, Prometheus remains defiant as Zeus buries him in a storm-shattered ravine; the Chorus stays with him.

l: Aeschylus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Aeschylus, a Greek dramatist, lived sixty-nine years, fought at Marathon and Salamis, and wrote nearly a hundred dramas; seven surviving plays remain major examples of early Greek drama.

l: Aeschylean drama, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: includes the Orestean Trilogy Aeschylean drama is characterized in this unit by grand language, religious speculation, political themes, battle imagery, and large theological or legendary designs. Several surviving plays are complete as poems but are fragments of lost trilogies.

l: the seven surviving dramas of Aeschylus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: has_count seven The seven surviving dramas are described as including The Suppliant Maidens, The Persians, The Seven against Thebes, Prometheus Bound, and the three plays of the Orestean Trilogy. Four of the seven translated in the volume are fragments of lost trilogies, while the Orestean Trilogy survives as a complete trilogy.

l: The Suppliant Maidens, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: A mythical drama, probably the earliest extant poetic drama, follows the Danaids fleeing Egypt to Argos, seeking sanctuary, and rejecting suitors' demand for forced marriage.

l: the Orestean Trilogy, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_composed_of the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Eumenides The Orestean Trilogy, comprising Agamemnon, The Libation-Bearers, and The Eumenides, is the only complete surviving example of an Aeschylean trilogy. The unit calls it the masterpiece of Aeschylean drama.

l: the Suppliant Maidens trilogy, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: includes The Suppliant Maidens [probably as its earliest surviving part] The Suppliant Maidens trilogy is reconstructed conjecturally from the surviving play and fragments. Its later parts may have shown the Danaids being reclaimed, killing their bridegrooms except for one, and ultimately being acquitted through the intervention of Aphrodite.

l: Danaus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Danaus is the son of Belus, descended through Io, Epaphus, and Libya, and the father, guide, and advocate of the Danaids. He leads his daughters from Egypt to Argos to escape the marriages sought by the sons of Aegyptus. At Argos, he directs them to seek sanctuary at the altars, display their suppliant wands, and speak modestly and submissively as an armed host approaches. He appeals for protection, requests guidance through the city, and is received as an honored elder and advocate. After the Argive vote secures protection, he reports the pursuing fleet, obtains armed aid, and counsels his daughters to honor Argos, preserve their reputation, and value chastity.

l: Chorus of the Daughters of Danaus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Chorus of the Daughters of Danaus is a collective group of Danaus’s daughters and suppliants. Descended from Io through Epaphus, Libya, and Belus, they regard Argos as their ancestral home. They flee Egypt with Danaus because they horrify at marriage to the sons of Aegyptus and seek protection from them in Argos. At sacred altars they appeal to Zeus, other gods, Pelasgus, and Justice, even threatening suicide if surrendered. After Danaus returns, they praise Argos and pray for its peace, prosperity, fertility, and freedom from plague and civic bloodshed. As pursuers approach, they express terror, resist the Herald, thank the King for intervening, and continue praying that Zeus will prevent the hated marriage.

l: the sons of Aegyptus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The sons of Aegyptus are a group of Aegyptus’s sons, first cousins and suitors of the daughters of Danaus. They desire marriage with the Danaids and claim a kinship-based right to them, but the women reject the union. Their wanton, violent pursuit drives the daughters and Danaus to flee from Egypt to Argos. The sons arrive or are expected by ship as armed adversaries to reclaim the Danaids for forced wedlock, creating a threat of conflict with Argos that may be settled through war and many deaths.

l: Argos, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Argos is a kingdom and land, also called Apian and Pelasgian land, ruled by Inachus and associated with Apis, who healed and cleansed it. It is the immemorial home of Io’s descendants, the ancestral land and refuge of Danaus and the Danaids, and contains the Argive shrines where they seek sanctuary after fleeing Egypt. Pelasgus and the citizens face the danger that either protecting or surrendering the suppliants could bring pollution, loss, or war. The people unanimously reject the suitors’ demand, shelter the Danaids, protect them from seizure, and lodge them within the fortified city. Later, Argos sends an alien armament against a city, and Argive forces are condemned for being brought against their fatherland.

l: Egypt, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Egypt is a land associated with the Nile. Io reaches it after wandering across distant lands and seas; Zeus restores her there, and she bears Epaphus. Later, Danaus and the Danaids flee Egypt because Aegyptus decrees forced marriages to his sons, who pursue them. The Danaids connect Egypt, the Syrian waste, and their return to their ancient Argive origin.

l: Aphrodite, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Aphrodite is a goddess of desire whose power governs love and sexual union, invoked in The Suppliant Maidens’ closing passages. As mother and queen of the Cadmean race, she later defends her prerogative and intervenes in the Danaids’ acquittal concerning their marriages.

l: the forced bridal of the Danaids, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The forced bridal of the Danaids is a hated, unwanted wedlock decreed by Aegyptus between his sons and the daughters of Danaus. The sons seek the marriages, but the Danaids reject them as imposed, loveless unions with kinsmen that would destroy their maidenhood. Horror at this threat drives the daughters’ flight from Egypt to Argos, where the action turns on whether Argos will protect them from pursuing suitors who seek to abduct them for marriage. The women pray for escape, preferring exile or death to the bridegrooms’ beds.

l: Atossa, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Atossa is the Persian queen-mother, widow and former consort of Darius, mother and royal patron of Xerxes, and resident of the Palace of Susa. In The Persians, she fears that Persia may collapse despite its wealth and numbers after dreams and omens warn of danger in Xerxes’ expedition. She consults the Persian Elders, questions a Messenger closely about the defeat, survivors, commanders, Greek ships, and battle, and responds with mourning, libations, prayers, and concern for Xerxes’ return. Through ritual mourning she summons Darius and gravely recounts Persia’s fall near Athens, Xerxes’ land-and-sea campaign, and his return from the Hellespont with only a remnant. After Darius departs, she fetches royal clothing to meet and comfort Xerxes in humiliation.

l: Xerxes, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Xerxes is a Persian king, son of Darius and Atossa, and royal heir. Young and reckless, he leads the Persian invasion of Greece and Hellas against Athens, commanding its army and fleet. He builds a bridge across the Hellespont to move his army, but his fleet is defeated at Salamis. Xerxes survives while witnessing the fleet’s destruction and the slaughter of chosen troops, then tears his royal robe, orders retreat, and flees in shame. He leaves Mardonius with three hundred thousand men; the army left behind is later destroyed near Plataea. Returning toward Susa in torn clothing with a nearly empty quiver, he mourns his dead commanders and soldiers and joins the Chorus in lamenting Persia’s defeat before entering the palace.

l: Darius, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Darius is a deceased former Persian king, husband of Atossa and father of Xerxes, remembered as wise and restrained, ruling Persia without military harm. After Persia’s catastrophe, Atossa and the Chorus summon his royal phantom from the underworld through libations and cries. He recognizes disaster as mortal fate, laments the consequences of Xerxes’ failed invasion, foretells the coming slaughter of Plataea, instructs that Xerxes be received ceremoniously, and returns to the shades.

l: the Persian Empire, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Persian Empire is an eastern Persian realm of great wealth centered at Susa. Under Xerxes, it sends wealth, forces, and ships against Hellas, but suffers a catastrophic defeat at Salamis. Much of its army, fleet, and leading men are lost; Persia mourns, its power to exact tribute and rule is weakened, and its former wealth, authority, and glory give way to bloodshed and ruin.

l: the Greco-Persian Wars, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Greco-Persian Wars provide the historical setting and subject matter for The Persians. The play was produced for a generation that had witnessed the conflicts at Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea.

l: the Battle of Marathon, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Marathon is the place where those who defeated Darius had previously defeated the Persians. Xerxes begins his campaign against Hellas to take vengeance for that defeat.

l: Persian defeat at Salamis, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Persian defeat at Salamis is a naval disaster commemorated in The Persians. In confined waters, Persian ships collide, lose oar-banks, overturn, and leave wrecks and dead men; Greek forces kill survivors. The battle destroys much of Xerxes’ fleet and army, sends him home without an escort, and causes Persia’s mourning and humiliation.

l: the Battle of Plataea, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Battle of Plataea is a land battle and Persian defeat, foretold as punishment for destroying Greek shrines and temples. Near Plataea, Lacedaemonians, Athenians, and Tegeans defeat Mardonius’s Persian force, destroying especially its rear guard.

l: The Seven against Thebes, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Seven against Thebes, the third part of the House of Laius trilogy, depicts defense of the Cadmea against Polynices and Argive allies, ending with Eteocles and Polynices dead, the male line extinct, and Antigone protesting Polynices' dishonorable treatment.

l: the House of Laius trilogy, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_also_called The House of Laius [collectively] The House of Laius trilogy is the collective design of which The Seven against Thebes is the third part. Its first two plays were probably called Laius and Oedipus, but they are lost.

l: Laius, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Laius, king of the Cadmeans and father of Oedipus, is warned by Apollo through the oracle of Delphi to remain childless to protect his house and land. He fathers Oedipus anyway, exposes the child on Mount Cithaeron, and is later killed unknowingly by his grown son.

l: Oedipus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Oedipus is the exposed son of Laius and Iokaste, saved and raised in Corinth by another king and queen. Trying to avoid an oracle, he unknowingly kills Laius, his father, and marries Iokaste, his mother. Once honored as king of Thebes for solving a fiend’s riddle and saving the city, he learns the truth and blinds himself. He is father of Eteocles and Polynices, whom he curses after being denied banquet honors. His curse afflicts his house and is fulfilled through the brothers’ deaths.

l: Iokaste, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Iokaste marries Laius and becomes the mother of Oedipus. After the revelation that she has married her son, she kills herself, while Oedipus tears out his eyes.

l: Eteocles, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Eteocles, son of Oedipus and Iokaste and twin brother of Polynices, is king and ruler of Cadmus’ folk. During the Argive siege, he commands the Cadmeans to arm, hold the walls, and resist fear. He selects defenders for the seven gates, dismisses the enemy champions’ boasts, and becomes the seventh defender. Though warned by the Chorus, he chooses to guard the seventh gate himself against Polynices, asserting his claims as ruler and brother. In single combat, the brothers kill one another. Because Eteocles defended Cadmus’ city, the state orders careful and honorable burial rites for him.

l: Polynices, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Polynices is a son of Oedipus and Iokaste and twin brother of Eteocles, described as an exiled claimant from Thebes. He leads Argive allies and foreign forces against Cadmus’ city, is assigned to the seventh gate, and vows to take the wall, reclaim his ancestral home, and fight Eteocles to the death. The brothers kill one another in single combat. Afterward, the city’s decree denies Polynices burial and orders his body cast out for dogs and birds, while Antigone vows to cover and bury him.

l: Antigone, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Antigone, daughter of Oedipus and sister of Eteocles and Polynices, mourns her brothers’ deaths. When a decree denies Polynices honorable burial, she defies it, approaching with Ismene and mourners to cover his body with dust. Her commitment to sisterhood and their shared birthright drives her action.

l: Ismene, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a sister of Antigone [one of the daughters of Oedipus] Ismene approaches with Antigone and a train of mourners bearing the bodies of Eteocles and Polynices. She joins in the mourning for her dead brothers, but no separate action by her is stated.

l: Thebes, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Thebes is a city, later named for an expanded city associated with the Cadmea, though its name is absent from the play despite the traditional title. Identified by that title as the city in the conflict, it is threatened by seven champions who vow to storm, sack, or burn it. Eteocles and chosen defenders guard its gates. The city survives, remains secure, is saved from servitude, and decrees burial for Eteocles but not Polynices.

l: the Cadmea, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Cadmea is Cadmus’s citadel and setting of The Seven against Thebes, defended by Eteocles and six against Polynices’ forces; Parthenopaeus vows to storm and sack it, bearing a Sphinx shield with a Cadmean victim.

l: the Cadmeans, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Cadmeans are Cadmus’ people and defenders of the Cadmea when an Argive army threatens their city. Eteocles urges their men to protect its walls, shrines, altars, and gates; frightened maidens fear war, and Eteocles saves them from the assault.

l: the Seven against Thebes war, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Seven against Thebes war is a conflict between Argos and Thebes, in which Polynices and Argive allies assault the Cadmea. Seven champions and an Argive army besiege the city with cavalry, shields, spears, stones, and axes; Theban defenders are chosen for each gate as the Chorus prays. The attack is repulsed, but Eteocles and Polynices kill each other, ending the male line of Laius.

l: Apollo, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Apollo is an exiled, oracle-giving god whose prophecy that Laius die childless is fulfilled through Oedipus and his descendants, and who determines the outcome of the seventh-gate battle.

l: the Sphinx, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a fiend [the monster that once shamed Thebes] The Sphinx is shown as the ravening fiend that once shamed the city. Her image appears on Parthenopaeus's shield, where she carries a Cadmean in her claws.

l: the curse of Laius, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The curse of Laius begins when Laius violates Apollo’s warning to die childless by fathering Oedipus. It brings ruin to his house: Oedipus kills Laius and marries Iokaste, their relationship is revealed, and their sons enter a fatal conflict.

l: Prometheus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Prometheus is a Titan, god, son of Iapetos, and benefactor of humanity. He aids Zeus during the gods’ strife, yet later champions mortal men against Zeus’s will. By stealth he gives fire to perishable men and provides hope, arts, knowledge, civilization, practical skills, medicine, divination, sacrifice, metals, letters, and handicrafts, transforming mortals from unseeing and unreasoning creatures into conscious, thinking beings. Zeus punishes him for these gifts: Hephaestus fastens, chains, and nails him to a mountain rock in the remote Scythian steppe, at the earth’s limit. Prometheus knowingly accepts this lasting torment but hates the gods’ repayment of kindness with wrong and defies Zeus without yielding. Possessing foreknowledge, he predicts Zeus’s future fall through a destined stratagem and knows the threatened marriage and how it may be prevented. He tells Io of her future, Zeus’s overthrow, and his own eventual release through a saviour descended from her. Although Hermes and Zeus threaten him, he refuses to disclose the secret until his bonds are loosed. The account ends with the rocky ravine shattered by storm and earthquake, burying him beneath the collapsing rocks as he declares Zeus unjust.

l: Zeus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Zeus is a god and supreme ruler of gods and men: son of Cronos, newly enthroned after overthrowing Cronos, governing from heaven with thunder, lightning, eagle, and authority over divine purpose and the Fates. In the records of Prometheus Bound, he is a harsh, suspicious tyrant whose self-sought rule is enforced through punishment. He condemns and binds Prometheus for aiding humanity, intends humanity's destruction early in his reign, and commands Hermes to force from Prometheus the secret of a marriage destined to bring Zeus down. Though powerful and ruthless, he cannot evade ordained fate; Prometheus foretells that Zeus's own counsels and a future marriage will produce a child who overcomes him, while also saying Zeus will someday need Prometheus and become milder. Elsewhere, Zeus is chiefly invoked as protector and arbiter: lord and guard of suppliants, strangers, kinship, guestright, purity, justice, and the balance of fate. The Danaids appeal to him for rescue from ravishment and hated marriage, trusting his will to accomplish its result and fearing his wrath against those who scorn divine claims. He punishes hubris and is called saviour and guardian of mortals' purity. He is also invoked through his bolt against enemies. His bond with Io links him to the Danaids: he loves and approaches her as a bull, her persecution and exile follow, and in Egypt he restores her by touch and fathers Epaphus. Through Io and Epaphus he becomes ancestor of the Danaids. Thus the records present both an all-powerful guardian sought by the distressed and a newly established ruler whose violence, tyranny, and threatened overthrow shape the conflict with Prometheus.

l: Hephaestus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Hephaestus, a god and Prometheus’s kin, possesses fire as craft and forge power; compelled by Zeus, he reluctantly binds the pitied Prometheus to a rock.

l: Strength, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Strength, an enforcer of Zeus, commands Hephaestus to bind Prometheus, rejects pity, and frames the punishment as proof of Zeus’s power over craft.

l: the sea nymphs, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: remain_with Prometheus [sharing his fate through the catastrophe] The sea nymphs form the Chorus of Prometheus Bound. They arrive in a winged car after hearing the sound of Prometheus's punishment, remain with him despite the danger, and refuse Hermes's demand that they withdraw before the final cataclysm.

l: Oceanus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Oceanus is a sea god and father of the Oceanides. Moved by kinship with Prometheus, he visits on a griffin, offers to seek Zeus’s relief, is warned of Zeus’s hatred, and leaves.

l: Io, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Io is a partly human daughter of Inachus, priestess of Hera in Argos, and beloved of Zeus. Hera’s jealousy transforms her into an ox-horned heifer and drives her into frenzy; Argus watches her as she wanders over lands and seas, suffering a divinely imposed affliction comparable to Prometheus’s punishment. Prometheus recounts her past and future wanderings before she departs again. Io eventually reaches Egypt, where Zeus restores her to sanity and human form by touch. She then gives birth to Epaphus and becomes ancestor of the daughters of Danaus, who claim descent through him.

l: Hera, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Hera is a goddess and queen of heaven, called upon for aid, who has power over Zeus together with Aphrodite. Most prominently, jealousy and hatred over Zeus’s love for Io drive her actions: she is said to transform Io into a heifer or cow-like form, appoint Argus to guard her, and create or send a gadfly. Through relentless wrath, malice, and poisonous hatred, Hera persecutes Io, driving her into frenzy, wandering, exile, and prolonged suffering. Her continuing anger is feared to afflict others as well.

l: Hermes, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Hermes is a god, Zeus’s herald and courier. He kills Argus by craft and serves as a herald’s champion. As Zeus’s messenger, he demands information from Prometheus about a marriage threatening Zeus, warns of burial and eagle torment, and fails to change Prometheus or the Chorus.

l: the gift of fire and civilization to humanity, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The gift of fire and civilization to humanity is Prometheus’s secret aid to oppressed mortals, who had lived without arts, science, letters, or handicrafts. By carrying fire to them, he becomes their teacher and chief resource, prompting Zeus to imprison and torment him.

l: gift, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: comes_from Time [from its grave] The gift is presented as coming from the grave of Time and from the shattered remains of ancient Greece. It carries the fragrance and living memories of vanished days.

l: Hellas, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Hellas is a western land of ancient memory, myth, poetry, and enduring spirit, figured as a mother to those with grave and fair dreams. Though its urns, cups, crowns, and tombs are broken, its memories survive. Persian forces advance against it under Xerxes, but Hellas protects Greeks: victory at Salamis and Plataea stops its subjugation, while scarcity and famine weaken the remaining invaders, who are punished for attacking its gods and temples.

l: Athens, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Athens is a Pallas-protected city, wealthy in silver mines and defended by men who fight with shields and spears without submitting to a master. Xerxes targets it for revenge, but its firm bulwark and powerful forces help bring about the Persian defeat.

l: Io, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Io, daughter of Inachus and ox-horned maiden in animal form, is loved by Zeus and harassed by Hera. Stung continually by a gadfly and driven mad, she reaches Prometheus’s prison seeking her fate. Her divinely inflicted transformation and wandering continue through many lands, including Bosporos and the Ionian Sea, until Egypt, where Zeus restores her reason; she bears Epaphus, founds a new abode, and becomes ancestress of the Danaids and ancestor of her future saviour.

l: Argus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Argus is an earth-born, many-eyed herdsman, described as malevolent, appointed by Hera to watch Io wherever she wanders. His myriad eyes serve this vigilance. In the end, Zeus wills and Hermes craft his death, separating Argus from life.

l: Epaphus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Epaphus is the child of Zeus and Io, born to Io after Zeus’s restoring, life-giving touch and named for that touch. He becomes king of Argos and fathers Libya. Through Libya, the Danaids trace their descent, and his descendants inherit Nile-enriched land.

l: Aegyptus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Aegyptus, son of Belus and brother of Danaus, descends from Io through Epaphus and Libya. He fathers sons and decrees they marry Danaus’s daughters, prompting the daughters’ flight from Egypt while his sons pursue them.

l: father of the maidens, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Danaus, father of the maidens, flees with them over the sea to Argos.

l: supplicant maidens, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The supplicant maidens, daughters of Danaus, flee the sons of Aegyptus because they reject marriage, reach Argos, and receive shelter and protection from its king and citizens.

l: Pelasgus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Pelasgus is the king and ruler of Argos and the Pelasgians, descended from Palaichthon. His central role is deciding whether Argos will protect the Danaids, a choice that could bring war with the sons of Aegyptus. When he appears, he questions the suppliants, recognizes their claim through Io, and delays a pledge until he can consult and persuade the Argive people. He later defends the sanctuary and the city’s will against the Herald, forbids the maidens’ removal by force, expels the Herald, and grants the Danaids shelter, protection, and hospitality.

l: the Argive people, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Argive people, citizens of Argos also called Pelasgians, constitute the commonwealth whose counsel Pelasgus must seek. Asked to judge the supplicant Danaids, they unanimously vote to shelter them, keep them free from violent seizure, provide Danaus armed escorts, and bind themselves by oath and public curse to protect the maidens.

l: the daughters of Danaus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The daughters of Danaus are a sister-band of suppliant maidens, descended from Io through Epaphus, who flee Egypt with their father to escape forced marriages to the sons of Aegyptus. Carrying wool-wound olive-shoots, they seek protection and chastity in Argos. The Argive people grant them protection; when the pursuing fleet arrives, they resist the Herald, cling to sanctuary, and are offered secure lodging in the city.

l: the herald of Aegyptus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: A herald representing Aegyptus’ sons claims the Danaids as property and tries to force them back to Aegyptus’ ship, rejecting local gods; the King of Argos stops him under an Argive decree and sends him away.

l: the sacred precinct near the gates of Argos, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: A sacred precinct near Argos’s gates, containing Zeus’s and other deities’ shrines and statues, where the daughters arrive, seek refuge, and prepare to defend suppliant status.

l: the shrines of Zeus and the other deities, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Argive shrines, a sacred precinct near Argos’s gates, are dedicated to gods as suppliant sites; Danaids sit there, and Pelasgus protects them, sending Danaus to city altars.

l: the Danaids’ flight from forced marriage, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Danaus and his daughters flee Egypt by sea to Argos to escape marriages imposed by the sons of Aegyptus. Choosing flight as the lesser grief, they pray for safety and freedom, then ask the king of Argos for protection from being dragged away.

l: suppliant protection, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_symbolized_by the olive-shoot [wool-enwound and carried in the left hand] The daughters seek suppliant protection from Zeus, the gods of Argos, and the rulers of the land. Danaus teaches them that the shrine and altar offer stronger protection than a tower and directs them to approach with meek and piteous words.

l: the olive-shoot, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The olive-shoot, wound with wool, is carried in the left hand as the weapon and sign of a suppliant. Danaus tells the daughters to hold their white-crowned wands reverently before those who question them.

l: the suppliant altar, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: provides suppliant protection [as a sacred refuge] The suppliant altar is a sacred place at which the daughters can seek safety from those pursuing them. Danaus orders them to cling to the altar-mound and crouch on holy ground like doves fleeing alien hawks.

l: the approaching Argive host, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a speared and shielded band [approaching the suppliants] Danaus sees dust, the sound of grinding axles, curved cars, horses, spears, and shields, indicating that an armed host is approaching. He thinks the chiefs of the land may be coming to inspect the suppliants, whether peacefully or with hostile intent.

l: Canopus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a town [at the verge of land and sea] Canopus is a town at the edge of land and sea where the Nile issues through silted sand. There Zeus will restore Io’s reason, and Io will bear Epaphus.

l: suppliant branches, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: New-plucked olive boughs mark the Danaids’ appeal on gods’ shrines; Pelasgus directs Danaus to place them at city altars, identifying the Danaids as suppliants.

l: the girdles, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: can_be_used_for suicide [by hanging the Danaids on the statues] The Danaids’ girdles and bands can be used to hang them from the statues of the gods. They threaten this act if Pelasgus does not give them a secure pledge against surrender.

l: the suppliants’ ritual, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The suppliants’ ritual involves sitting beside sacred shrines, laying down olive branches, and appealing to the gods and the ruler for protection. Pelasgus treats these signs as a serious religious obligation and seeks to make the whole city aware of them.

l: the threatened war between Argos and Aegyptus’ sons, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: A threatened war between the Argive people and Aegyptus’ sons arises over the Danaids. Pelasgus fears both conflict if Argos protects them and divine pollution if it surrenders them. The Herald invokes Ares rather than testimony, and the approaching fleet threatens corpses and many deaths.

l: Io’s transformation and wanderings, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Io is transformed into a horned heifer and exiled from Argos, guarded by Argus and driven by Hera’s gadfly through Greece, Asia, Phrygia, Mysia, Lydia, Cilicia, Pamphylia, and Egypt. Zeus restores her human form, and she bears Epaphus.

l: the gadfly, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a scourge [of divine infliction] The gadfly is the stinging scourge that drives Io into frenzy and forces her to roam the world. Its repeated sting causes her renewed cries of pain and madness.

l: Justice, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Justice is a maiden-child and daughter of Zeus, queen of suppliants, and a personified force of right dealing. The Danaids invoke her as Pelasgus weighs justice against his city's safety. Later, she is depicted on Polynices's shield promising restoration, but Eteocles rejects her support for his impious attack.

l: the will of Zeus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: governs counsel [directing every device and decision] The will of Zeus is presented as governing the balance of good and evil, the fate of suppliants, and the movement of every counsel and deed. The Danaids trust that Zeus will punish those who deny justice and protect those who show grace to suppliants.

l: Pelasgian land, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: provides the city’s protection [to suppliant strangers] The Pelasgian land is described as having pitied and protected the suppliant Danaids. The Chorus prays that it will not be devastated by war, disease, corpses, or civic bloodshed.

l: the sanctuary, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a sacred refuge [under the protection of the gods] The sanctuary is the refuge to which the Danaids cling when the Herald of Aegyptus tries to remove them. The King of Argos treats interference with it as an insult to the gods and forbids the Herald to use force there.

l: the pursuing fleet, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a fleet of ships [sent to recover the Danaids] The pursuing fleet is seen approaching with spread canvas, multiple ships, painted prows, and crews identified as the Danaids’ pursuers. Its arrival causes the Danaids to fear capture, forced marriage, and war.

l: the ships, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: belong_to the sons of Aegyptus [as their pursuing transport] The ships of the pursuers come toward the shore under oars after furling their sails. Danaus argues that anchoring and disembarking will take time, giving the Argives an opportunity to provide aid.

l: the Argive decree protecting the maidens, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: forbids the threatened forced marriage [by prohibiting forcible removal] The decree states that the maidens may remain in the land free from seizure or violation, and that no native or foreign hand may drag them away. Anyone among the countrymen who fails to aid them is threatened with the people’s curse and banishment.

l: the vote of the Argives, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: establishes the Argive decree protecting the maidens [by unanimous public decision] The Argives’ vote is made with one assent in full conclave and without a herald’s proclamation. Through it, the people resolve to protect the Danaids and to support Zeus’s concern for suppliants and strangers.

l: the Fates, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Fates are triform powers governing destiny: they ordain Prometheus’s inescapable punishment, govern Xerxes, and through divine intervention cause Persia’s defeat. They bring overwhelming disaster and ruin, fulfilling an oracle and divine presage as Xerxes advances toward fate.

l: the city, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a Pelasgian city [granting refuge and protection to the Danaids] The city votes to protect the Danaids and is warned that mistreating suppliants who are also kin would bring divine enmity and a twofold curse. The Chorus prays that the city will remain fertile, peaceful, well-governed, and free from disease and internal violence.

l: the city’s protection, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a public defense [granted to Danaus and the Danaids] The city’s protection prevents the Herald of Aegyptus from taking the Danaids by force. It includes the Argive decree, armed support for Danaus, and the King’s promise that the maidens will be guarded within the city.

l: the Argive city’s hospitality, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: includes shelter for the Danaids [in the king’s or people’s dwellings] The King offers the Danaids a choice between lodging in the king’s palace or in separate homes within the fortified city. He promises that they will find a welcome and loyal protection from the people.

l: Chorus of Persian Elders, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Chorus of Persian Elders is a group of aged men of Susa, representing the Persian community and appointed as royal warders to guard Xerxes’ wealth and advise the household. It anxiously awaits news of the army, recounts its movement into Hellas, and interprets Atossa’s dream. After the messenger announces disaster, it laments Persia’s dead, widows, ruined cities, and broken kingship, summons Darius’ ghost, recalls his prosperous reign, mourns with Xerxes, and leads him back to the palace.

l: Persian armament, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Persian armament, a Persian host marshalled for war, includes fleet, cavalry, bowmen, and chariots as it crosses Asia toward Hellas; Chorus fears its loss and desolation in Persia.

l: Persian army, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Persian army invades Hellas under Xerxes, crosses the bridge across the Hellespont, and suffers defeat at Salamis in a naval disaster. As it retreats through Greece and Thrace, hunger, thirst, pursuit, drought, and freezing reduce it to a small remnant. Xerxes leaves three hundred thousand men under Mardonius to fight by land; this remaining force is destroyed near Plataea by the Lacedaemonians, Athenians, and Tegeans.

l: Greeks, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Greeks resist the Persian invasion by land and sea to defend Athens and freedom. They remain by their ships overnight, attack at dawn calling for freedom, country, families, temples, and ancestral graves, defeat Persian ships at Salamis, assault troops on a nearby islet, and destroy Mardonius’ army near Plataea. Their victories prompt a warning that Persia should not attack Greek lands again.

l: Athenians, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Athenians are a fighting group central to Persian defeat: with allied forces they defeat the fleet at Salamis, then join Lacedaemonians and Tegeans near Plataea to destroy the army. They fight with shields and spears without bowing as slaves; their city and ancestral Athens become a warning against excessive pride.

l: Susa, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Susa is a Persian city and seat of the royal palace, where the Chorus and royal household await news of Xerxes' army; as defeat becomes clear, it mourns the unprecedented loss of its warriors.

l: Palace of Susa, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a royal palace [scene of the drama] The scene is set at the Palace of Susa, where the Chorus guards royal wealth and Atossa seeks counsel. A Persian courier arrives there with news of good or ill for Persia.

l: Salamis, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Salamis is an island near and fronting Athens, also a naval battlefield and strait. Its Cychrea Bay is associated with the dead. Persian ships are shattered, sunk, or routed there by Athens, Lacedaemon, Aegina, and Corinth; its beaches, reefs, waters, and nearby islet become filled with wreckage and Persian dead as soldiers and commanders are lost.

l: Hellespont, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Hellespont is a sea strait whose waters Xerxes’ forces cross on a frail bridge of cordage, rope, and planking. Storms make the passage perilous, and Darius condemns the bridge as mad defiance of divine power.

l: Plataea, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Plataea, in Boeotia, is a battlefield where the Persian rear guard and Xerxes’ army left under Mardonius are destroyed by Lacedaemonians, Athenians, and Tegeans; Darius foretells widespread death there as testimony against mortal pride.

l: Ionian lands, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Xerxes goes to war in the Ionian lands, according to Atossa’s account of her recurring visions. The dream associates the Ionian-dressed woman with the obedient team member who submits to the chariot’s reins.

l: Salamis naval battle, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Salamis naval battle begins when the Persian fleet is deceived into expecting a Greek flight. At dawn Athens and its allies attack; Persian ships jammed in the strait are rammed, disabled, overturned, shattered, sunk, or put to flight until night, causing Persian defeat and Xerxes' return toward Susa.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Persian invasion of Greece is Xerxes’ military expedition against Hellas, launched to avenge Darius’ defeat at Marathon and to destroy Athens and lay Hellas low. Xerxes leads an enormous army and fleet, building a bridge across the Hellespont. The campaign ends disastrously at Salamis and near Plataea, with vast losses, Persian glory collapsing, and Xerxes fleeing in shame.

l: bridge over the Hellespont, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: A bridge built by Xerxes across the Hellespont enables Persian land forces to pass from Asia into Hellas/Europe. Made with carpentry, cordage, and planking, it is vulnerable to sea and wind. The Chorus notes its weakness, and Darius condemns it as mortal defiance of divine power.

l: Persian fleet, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Persian fleet is a Persian naval force larger than the Greek fleet, accompanying the invasion and gathering between Athens and Salamis. Though more than a thousand ships strong, it is trapped in the narrowing strait, battered and wrecked by Greek ships, and ultimately destroyed, sunk, or forced to flee.

l: Darius’ ghost, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a phantom from the grave [summoned by Atossa] Darius’ ghost is invoked as a possible source of help for Atossa, Xerxes, and Persia. The Chorus asks Atossa to pour offerings to the dead and call Darius forth from beneath the earth.

l: Ghost of Darius, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Ghost of Darius is a dead former Persian king, royal ancestor, father of Xerxes, sole ruler, and army leader. In The Persians, Atossa’s grief and the Chorus’s prayers and libations summon him after Xerxes’ defeat. Learning the army is destroyed, he condemns Xerxes’ recklessness, pride, and impiety, and warns Persia never again to attack Greek lands.

l: the gods, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: determine fate [as understood by Atossa and the chorus] The gods are regarded as having thwarted Persia’s purpose and brought disaster upon the army and fleet. Atossa prays to them and performs rites in hope of alleviating the consequences of the defeat.

l: Atossa’s dream, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Atossa’s dream is a vision portending Xerxes’ defeat: two noble women yoked to his chariot struggle, the Dorian breaks free and he falls; an eagle is attacked by a falcon, while Darius laments.

l: omens and prophecy, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Atossa experiences troubling dreams and sees an eagle attacked and overcome by a falcon at Phoebus’ shrine. The Chorus advises her to offer prayers and sacrifices to avert the predicted misfortune, while Atossa fears that defeat may threaten Xerxes and Persia.

l: Persian kingship and power, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Persian kingship and power is imperial authority marked by wealth, vast forces, royal command, and rule over many peoples. After defeat at Salamis, the loss of men and the king’s wrecked forces overturn that authority: the state cannot be preserved, subjects no longer crouch or obey Xerxes as before.

l: Athenian political freedom, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a freedom from slavery [Athenians acknowledge no master] The Chorus says that the Athenians do not bow as slaves to any man and do not acknowledge a master’s hand. Their lack of a single shepherd is presented as a striking contrast with Persian royal command.

l: messenger, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: A Persian courier and survivor returns from Salamis to the Palace of Susa. After arriving with uncertain news, he reports Persia’s defeat: the fleet’s destruction, commanders’ deaths, slaughter on the islet, and the land force’s disastrous retreat. Xerxes survives but flees after seeing the ruin.

l: Greek fleet, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Greek naval force of about three hundred galleys and ten select ships advances in order, exploits confined waters, and destroys the larger Persian fleet by ramming and encirclement at Salamis.

l: Persian defeat, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: results_from shipwreck and slaughter at Salamis [with the Persian fleet destroyed] The Persian defeat destroys the fleet, kills many commanders and soldiers, and forces Xerxes and the survivors into a desperate retreat. The defeat also brings mourning across the Persian land and breaks confidence in Persian power.

l: Darius’s summoning, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a funerary invocation [performed for counsel and relief] Atossa pours milk, honey, water, wine, olive fruit, and flowers as libations for Darius. The CHORUS calls upon Earth, Hermes, and the king of Hades to release Darius so that he may return and speak about Persia’s suffering.

l: freedom of Greece, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: motivates Greeks [in battle at Salamis] The Greek battle song presents the fight as a struggle for the freedom of Greece, urging the Greeks to defend their country, families, temples, and ancestral graves. The Greek victory prevents Persian domination of Hellas.

l: Persian people, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Persian people, ruled by Darius, suffer defeat at Salamis and mourn fallen warriors, enduring ruin across Persia and losing confidence, glory, and military strength.

l: Ionians, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: defeat Persian army [with naval forces at Salamis] The Ionians fight against the Persians and gain glory in the battle at sea. Xerxes says that Ionian ships harvest victory in the bay, and the Chorus declares that the Ionian power has helped bring Persia’s ruin.

l: hubris, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: causes Persian defeat at Salamis [as divine retribution] Hubris appears in Xerxes’ belief that he could control the Helle and in the Persian destruction of Greek religious images and temples. Darius warns that excessive pride brings divine punishment, tears, and the loss of prosperity.

l: THE SPY, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Spy is a scout and messenger sent to observe the Argive camp. He personally sees seven warriors swear to destroy Cadmus’ city or die, warns Eteocles of their armed advance, and reports each champion assigned to a gate, including their boasts, shields, and threats. After the assault, he announces that the city, its walls, and gates are safe, but that Eteocles and Polynices killed each other at the seventh gate.

l: Chorus of Cadmean maidens, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: A chorus of maidens from Cadmus’ city fears the Argive army’s victory, cries and prays for protection, and, despite Eteocles’ condemnation, warns of slaughter, slavery, and forced marriage.

l: Argives, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Argives are an invading army led by seven warriors, advancing with assault forces and equipment to surround, press, and besiege Cadmus’ city and its seven gates.

l: the seven warriors, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The seven warriors are powerful Argive chiefs who sacrifice a bull’s blood and swear to raze Cadmus’ walls or die trying. They cast lots for the seven gates, then lead their companies toward the city.

l: the gods, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The gods protect Cadmus’ city during the Argive assault, invoked by Eteocles and the Chorus, and are promised sacrifices and enemy armor for victory.

l: Cadmus’ city, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Cadmus’ city, held by Cadmus and the Cadmeans, is besieged during the war by Argives seeking to raze and control it; its defenders ready the gates and walls amid fears of sack and enslavement.

l: the seven gates, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: belong_to Cadmus’ city [its defended gates] The seven gates are the points at which the Argive assault is directed. Eteocles intends to place six chosen men and himself at the gates to confront the seven attacking companies.

l: the curse of Oedipus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The curse of Oedipus is a paternal imprecation and prophetic force over his sons Eteocles and Polynices. It declares that they will divide their kingdom or inheritance by iron and the sword rather than gold, governing their fate and driving them into mortal conflict. It remains effective until its fulfillment: the brothers fight, kill each other, and their mutual deaths realize the ancient family doom.

l: slavery, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: threatens Cadmus’ city [if the Argives prevail] Slavery is presented as a feared consequence if the Argives capture Cadmus’ city. Eteocles calls for the land to remain free, while the Chorus imagines the city’s women being taken and subjected to the conquerors.

l: the city’s defense, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_led_by Eteocles [with six chosen men] The city’s defense depends on armed men taking positions at the walls, bulwarks, towers, and gates. Eteocles organizes the defense, trusts in scouts and plans, and personally leads six men as the seventh defender.

l: the Six Champions, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a defenders of Thebes [posted at the gates against the attackers] The six champions opposing the first six gates are Tydeus, Capaneus, Eteoclus, Hippomedon, Parthenopaeus, and Amphiaraus. The Spy reports their assignments, weapons, boasts, and shield devices, while Eteocles selects defenders against them.

l: the Chorus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Chorus prays for the city's safety and fears that the champions will return as blood-stained wrecks. It warns Eteocles not to meet Polynices at the seventh gate and laments the inherited curse, family bloodshed, and pollution threatening the house of Oedipus.

l: Tydeus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Tydeus, an Argive warrior assigned to attack the Proetides gate, storms it with violent eagerness, displaying plumes, bells, and a shield bearing the nightly sky, stars, and full moon, while Amphiaraus opposes and restrains him by prophetic judgment.

l: Amphiaraus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Amphiaraus, a seer and prophet deemed wisest and bravest among warriors, restrains and rebukes Tydeus, guards the Homoloid gate as an enemy champion, and, foreknowing his death, accepts an honorable end.

l: Capaneus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a Argive champion [attacking the Electran gates] Capaneus is assigned to the Electran gates and boasts that neither gods nor Zeus's warrior maid can stop him from destroying the city. His shield shows a weaponless man carrying a torch with the words "Fire for the city bring I"; Eteocles sets Polyphontes against him.

l: Hippomedon, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Hippomedon is an Argive champion assigned to attack Pallas Onca’s portal, bearing Typhon on his smoke-emitting, snake-ringed shield; Eteocles counters him by assigning Hyperbius, whose shield bears Zeus.

l: Hyperbius, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Hyperbius, son of Oenops, is chosen as Thebes’ defender against Hippomedon, bearing Zeus on his shield to oppose Hippomedon’s Typhon.

l: Parthenopaeus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: bears the Sphinx [as the device on his shield] Parthenopaeus is assigned to the northern gate before the death-mound of Amphion. Though young and beautiful, he is fierce and vows to storm the Cadmean stronghold; his shield bears the ravening Sphinx carrying a Cadmean in its claws, and Actor is chosen to oppose him.

l: the Fury, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a house-fiend [embodiment of inherited vengeance] The Fury is described as the black-robed force of the family curse, driving the children toward their doom. The Chorus asks that she leave the house when the gods accept a votive offering, but Eteocles says the curse has already made her urgent.

l: the seventh gate, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_defended_by Eteocles [against Polynices] The seventh gate is assigned to Polynices, while Eteocles resolves to defend it personally. It becomes the place where the brothers are expected to meet in combat.

l: the shields of the champions, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: bear the seven shield devices [symbolic devices identifying the warriors] The shields display the champions' boasts and intended acts through elaborate devices and inscriptions. Their emblems include the starry sky, a torch, a scaling warrior, Typhon, the Sphinx, a plain bronze surface, and Justice leading a warrior.

l: the seven shield devices, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The seven devices are the starry heavens and full moon on Tydeus's shield, the torch-bearing man on Capaneus's, the scaling warrior on Eteoclus's, Typhon on Hippomedon's, the Sphinx on Parthenopaeus's, no device on Amphiaraus's, and Justice leading a warrior on Polynices's.

l: the prophecy of Loxias, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: foretells the death of Amphiaraus [according to Eteocles’ interpretation] Eteocles refers to Loxias's prophecy when he says Amphiaraus knows the outcome of the struggle and therefore will not assail the gate in the ordinary way. The prophecy is presented as something that will be fulfilled through the battle.

l: the confrontation of Eteocles and Polynices, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The confrontation of Eteocles and Polynices is a cursed brotherly combat at the seventh gate. Eteocles meets Polynices as ruler, rival, and brother despite the Chorus’s warning. They strike each other dead with swords, ending their conflict and saving the city, but leaving their house and the Chorus grieving.

l: the inherited family pollution, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: originates_in the house of Oedipus [arising from incest, parricide, and ancestral curses] The inherited family pollution arises from the old sins of Laius, Oedipus, and their house and passes from one generation to the next. The Chorus asks who can purify the blood shed when kin meet kin, declaring that the ancient pollution rises again through the coming battle.

l: Chorus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Chorus is a group of sea-nymphs, daughters of Oceanus, who worship Oceanus and appear as compassionate gods and supplicants seeking knowledge from Prometheus. In Prometheus Bound, they arrive in winged cars after hearing his punishment, pity and support him, and listen as he describes Zeus’s hidden, implacable rule. They mourn his suffering, recall his gifts to mortals, compare him with Atlas, and warn him not to offend Zeus. They question him about Io and his eventual release, horror-struck by Io’s fate. Though they urge him to yield, they reject Hermes’s charge of cowardice and remain loyally beside Prometheus. In the burial crisis after Eteocles and Polynices die, they grieve Oedipus’ cursed line and divide between Antigone’s burial of Polynices and Eteocles’ funeral.

l: Herald, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a official messenger [speaking for the counsellors of Cadmus’ town] The Herald announces the state’s burial orders: Eteocles is to receive proper burial, while Polynices is to be denied burial and left for birds and dogs. He forbids Antigone from burying Polynices, but she rejects his command.

l: the Furies, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Furies, unforgiving avenging powers, bring the curse of Oedipus to completion through the brothers’ deaths, embodying inherited ruin and violence.

l: foreign enemy forces, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Foreign enemy forces attack Cadmus’ city alongside Polynices. They are repelled, and the city is saved from a foreign yoke.

l: the seventh-gate battle, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a battle [at the seventh gate] At the seventh gate, Eteocles and Polynices meet in combat and kill each other. THE SPY connects the battle with Apollo and the fulfillment of the doom upon Oedipus’ sons.

l: the state burial decree, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Cadmus’s counsellors issue a decree honoring Eteocles with burial and exposing Polynices; Antigone openly defies it as the Chorus is divided over obedience.

l: burial rites, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Eteocles is to receive burial with care, mourners, ritual, and honor. Polynices is denied women-wailers, a tomb, a dirge, and attendance, though Antigone and part of the Chorus undertake to provide him burial.

l: the sword, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: causes the mutual slaughter of Eteocles and Polynices [as the arbiter of their dispute] The sword serves as the arbitrator of the brothers’ dispute and gives both Eteocles and Polynices their deathblows. The Chorus condemns the sword as both the instrument of their deaths and the divider of their lives.

l: the unburied body of Polynices, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a corpse [denied public burial] The unburied body of Polynices is ordered to be left for dogs and birds without tomb, lament, or funeral escort. Antigone refuses to accept this treatment and prepares to cover the body with light dust.

l: gods, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The gods are divided between supporters of Cronos and Zeus; with Prometheus’s help, Zeus prevails. Under Zeus, his subservient followers fear the new ruler and do not pity Prometheus. Prometheus recalls two fallen dynasties, expects a third tyrannical one to fall, and condemns the gods’ ingratitude.

l: mortal men, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Mortal men begin as a purblind, artless race, living in caves without understanding, reason, or foresight, while Zeus intends their destruction. Prometheus saves them, gives fire and blind hopes, and instructs them in consciousness, practical arts, medicine, divination, sacrifice, and metal use.

l: Scythian steppe, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The Scythian steppe is described as the earth’s boundary, a waste untrodden by men. It is the remote region where Prometheus is bound.

l: the Caucasus-like rocky ravine, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The rocky ravine in the mountains of Scythia contains the steep rock to which Prometheus is fastened. It is a desolate prison exposed to sun, wind, cold, and solitude. The rocky ravine is the place where Prometheus is bound and confronted by Hermes. Zeus’s thunder and lightning rend its crags, and the shattered rocks fall to bury Prometheus.

l: the stolen fire, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: enables arts [of mortal men] Prometheus secretly steals fire in a fennel-stalk and gives it to mortal men. Fire enables them to learn many arts, and Zeus punishes Prometheus for this gift.

l: human arts and knowledge, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Prometheus gives mortal men arts that aid their prosperity on earth. He connects these arts with the fire he secretly provides. Human arts and knowledge include writing, number, memory, song, astronomy, carpentry, animal training, chariot and seafaring technology, medicinal drugs, divination, interpretation of omens, sacrificial practice, and the discovery of copper, iron, silver, and gold. These arts were unknown or undeveloped among mortals until Prometheus taught or devised them.

l: hope, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Prometheus sends blind hopes to nestle in the hearts of mortal men. The Chorus regards this as a goodly gift that helps them endure their mortal condition.

l: tyranny, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_characterized_by suspicion of friends [in a ruler] Tyranny is presented as the inward vice of treating friends as secret foes. Prometheus identifies Zeus’s new rule as tyranny because Zeus rewards his former ally with punishment and trusts only his own will.

l: compassion, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_denied_to Prometheus [by Zeus’s punishment] Prometheus’s compassion for mortal men leads him to oppose Zeus and rescue them from destruction. His compassion is not returned by Zeus, who makes him suffer despite his aid to humanity.

l: Prometheus’s punishment, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Prometheus’s punishment is an age-long ordeal imposed by Zeus for giving fire to men. Bound and immured in a Caucasus-like rocky ravine, he endures exposure, solitude, helplessness, anguish, and countless woes. He remains in fetters, believing art cannot overcome destiny and that release depends on Fate, the Furies, and Zeus’s will. The ordeal begins with his bondage on the rock; Hermes then foretells that collapsing rocks will bury him and that Zeus’s eagle will repeatedly tear and consume his flesh. It lasts without a stated natural limit, ending only when Zeus allows it or another deity bears the doom.

l: binding of Prometheus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Prometheus is bound by Hephaestus with permanent adamantine restraints and a wedge through his body, while Strength oversees and demands merciless, unwavering completion.

l: destruction of humanity, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Destruction of humanity is Zeus’s intended response to his contempt for mortal men. Prometheus alone opposes Zeus’s will and rescues mortal men from crushing ruin and the abyss of hell.

l: Prometheus’s fetters, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Prometheus’s fetters are adamant chains made by Hephaestus that fasten Prometheus to a rocky cleft by Zeus’s command, expressing Zeus’s power until Prometheus is released and they yield.

l: the future fall of Zeus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The future fall of Zeus is a foretold, threatened event in which Zeus loses pride, sway, and kingship. Prometheus predicts it will result from Zeus’s mindless counsels and a marriage, threatened according to Prometheus, that produces a child destined to overcome his sire and fulfill Cronos’s curse. Prometheus withholds knowledge of the destined stratagem until Zeus abandons his purpose and makes amends; a mighty being will arise able to overcome Zeus’s lightning and Poseidon’s trident.

l: Caucasus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: is_a world-topping peak [with a river descending from it] The Caucasus is the mountain peak Io must reach after crossing the Stream of Violence. Its heights overtop the world, and a river descends from them in spray.

l: Prometheus's aid to mortals, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Prometheus aids mortals by teaching arts: understanding stars, numbers, writing, memory, song, animal harnessing, chariots, ships, medicine, prophecy, omens, sacrifice, construction, and metals. The aid proceeds through these gifts and ends with metals stored in the earth, presented as a complete body of arts for mortal use.

l: Io’s wandering, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: Io’s wandering begins when Inachus expels her under the command of the oracle and Zeus’s threat. Prometheus maps her future route through Scythia, the Caucasus, the lands of the Amazons, Asia, the Gorgon-haunted regions, and finally Egypt.

l: Io’s future childbearing, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: At Canopus, Zeus will restore Io’s reason, and she will bear Epaphus. From Epaphus’s line will come later generations, including the descendant whose lineage will produce a hero who frees Prometheus.

l: the storm and earthquake, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: The storm and earthquake mark Zeus’s immediate punishment of Prometheus. Thunder, lightning, upheaving earth, whirlwinds, dust, battling storm clouds, and a heaving sea combine as the rocks are broken and brought down.

l: the threatened marriage of Zeus, Four Plays of Aeschylus
s: causes Zeus's fall from power [destined to bring about his overthrow] Prometheus refuses to identify the marriage that he says will cause Zeus to fall from supremacy. He claims that only he knows the means by which Zeus can avert the resulting ruin, while Hermes is sent to force the secret from him.

l: The Rhesus of Euripides
s: This document is a Project Gutenberg eBook of The Rhesus of Euripides, translated into English rhyming verse with explanatory notes by Gilbert Murray. The printed edition appeared in London through George Allen & Company, Ltd., in 1913; the eBook was released in 2011 and updated in 2021. Its front matter also lists other works and editions, and a transcriber’s note explains that line numbers follow the Greek text, records a correction, and describes minor editorial treatment. Murray’s introduction asks whether Rhesus is genuinely by Euripides or by a later anonymous poet. It considers manuscript, performance, linguistic, and stylistic evidence, especially comparisons with Alcestis and Cyclops. While most scholars are said to favor a fourth-century archaistic work, the introduction allows that it may be an early, pro-satyric Euripidean play later revised or reproduced by Euripides the Younger. It identifies the Doloneia as the source of the plot and presents Rhesus as a divine Thracian king associated with Pangaion. The drama begins after a Trojan and allied victory. Seeing signals and confusion among the Greeks, Hector considers attacking, but Aeneas urges reconnaissance. Dolon agrees to spy in a wolf disguise if he can receive Achilles’ horses. A shepherd then announces the arrival of Rhesus and his richly armed Thracian force. Rhesus enters in white armour, vows to destroy the Greek ships and end Troy’s suffering, and is reproached by Hector for arriving late; he answers that Scythian attacks delayed him. As dawn nears, Odysseus and Diomede enter on a night raid. Unable to find Hector, they receive Athena’s direction to kill Rhesus and seize his white horses. Athena deceives Paris so that the Greeks can escape. The Thracian camp is struck while asleep: Rhesus is killed and his horses taken. His wounded Charioteer initially blames Hector, but Hector attributes the deed to Odysseus. The Muse arrives with Rhesus’s body, curses the Greeks, Helen, and Athena, and declares that Rhesus will avoid ordinary burial and live as a spirit. Hector orders burial, promises aid to the Charioteer, and readies Troy for battle. The notes connect the play closely to the Iliad and the Doloneia, discuss staging and its portrayal of Trojans, Greeks, Lycians, and Thracians, and emphasize an ending in which hidden burial and renewed warfare remain overshadowed by disaster. The document closes with the Project Gutenberg License and information about use, distribution, liability, and support for the Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation.

l: The Rhesus of Euripides, The Rhesus of Euripides
s: The Rhesus of Euripides is a Greek tragedy and Project Gutenberg electronic work: a play translated by Gilbert Murray into English rhyming verse, with his explanatory notes, from a 1913 London edition. It is attributed to Euripides in manuscripts and ancient performance records, though its introduction emphasizes its early, severe, direct, grandiose style, rare words, Euripidean expressions, and imitation of Aeschylus; it also records three alternative openings and later reproductions. Closely based on and following the Doloneia, it presupposes knowledge of the Iliad and is set through one night in the Trojan camp. The action begins with the camp’s watch and the Watchers’ Song, includes the mission of Dolon and the arrival of Rhesus, a divine Thracian king of radiant martial splendour, son of the greatest River and a nameless Muse of the Mountain. Odysseus and Diomedes then attack; Rhesus’s death is central, alongside guards, spies, wolf-skin tokens, and divine appearances. The play ends with the Trojans’ final departure.

l: Euripides, The Rhesus of Euripides
s: Euripides is presented as an author and playwright associated with Rhesus, Alcestis, and Peliades, the last credited with his first victory. He is identified in front matter and by manuscripts, performance records, and early Alexandrian quotations as author of a Rhesus, though its style has prompted doubts. An introduction proposes an early pro-satyric work later reproduced or adapted after his death, possibly involving his son Euripides the Younger. Notes associate his work with forceful speeches, psychological conflict, lyricism, and daring, sometimes crude technique. Later listings represent him through several plays and lost tragedies.
